title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Warren enacts 12-month moratorium as Michigan towns weigh power, water and tax tradeoffs.

lines.text: Good evening and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy, the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're diving into Warren's brand-new year-long halt on data center proposals and what it signals for communities across the state.
That's right, Graham. Warren City Council just approved that 12-month moratorium today, and residents in Macomb County have been vocal about the power and water strain these projects could bring.
Exactly. This gives officials time to study zoning rules before any large facilities move forward. It's the latest in a string of local actions we've seen this week.
So why Warren now, and why does a single city's pause matter to folks 30 or 60 miles away?

Great question. Data centers are massive electricity users, sometimes hundreds of megawatts each, and they can pull millions of gallons of water daily for cooling. Warren's move is a direct response to those concerns.
I've heard the numbers thrown around, but walk me through what a gigawatt-scale facility actually means for the local grid and rates.

One large campus can equal the power draw of a small city. Utilities have warned that adding several at once risks higher bills for everyone as they build new generation and transmission. Warren's pause buys time to model those impacts.
And water? How big is that piece of the puzzle in southeast Michigan?

Cooling towers can consume enormous volumes, especially in summer. Macomb County residents have flagged aquifer stress and competition with farms and homes. The moratorium lets the city run the numbers on that too.
This isn't happening in isolation though. We saw Ypsilanti extend its freeze yesterday and Kalamazoo adding rules to its zoning code over the weekend.

Right. Springfield Township is facing a recall effort over fast-tracking concerns, and Saline Township delayed a big tax break vote for an Oracle project on Sunday. It's a pattern of communities hitting pause.
Why are so many places acting at once? Is it just the AI boom or something more local?

Both. Hyperscale demand is surging, but Michigan's older grid and limited water in some areas make it feel immediate. Townships are realizing approvals now lock in decades of impacts on roads, taxes and reliability.
What happens next in Warren specifically? Do they have a timeline for new rules?

The 12 months are for studying zoning. Expect public meetings, consultant reports on power and water, and eventually updated ordinances. Similar processes are underway in Garfield Township and elsewhere.
And for residents worried about farmland or property values, how does a moratorium help or hurt?
It prevents rushed approvals on prime land while giving everyone a voice. But developers may shift focus to more permissive areas, so the pressure just moves around the region.
We've also got Mason County breaking ground on two centers this past Saturday. How does that contrast with the pauses we're seeing?
Western Michigan is moving forward with construction jobs and tax revenue in mind, while southeast Michigan is more cautious. Different priorities, same underlying grid and water questions.
That developer restarting the old Emerson Electric site bid on Saturday, does that change anything for nearby towns?
It revives an old industrial footprint, which could limit new land use but still adds heavy power demand. Locals will watch the tax revenue versus rate impact debate closely.
Quick hits time. Let's start with the recall push in Springfield Township that surfaced yesterday.
Residents are gathering signatures to recall the supervisor they say fast-tracked projects that could strain roads, power and water. A successful recall would shift who controls future approvals.
Ypsilanti extended its freeze yesterday too. Any ripple effects for Ann Arbor or beyond?
The city council is keeping the moratorium while studying impacts. If big projects get approved later, regional electricity rates could feel it 30 miles away.
Saline Township postponed its vote on that 12-year tax break for Oracle on Sunday.
Supervisors delayed action on the abatement that would forgive taxes on a multibillion-dollar campus. Residents are questioning the revenue loss versus promised jobs.
Kalamazoo added a moratorium to its zoning code over the weekend.
Officials are writing in a temporary ban as AI proposals multiply, giving time to study power, land and noise effects.
Garfield Township is taking a full year to craft rules, announced Friday.
Supervisors in Grand Traverse County will draft zoning and permitting standards. Locals get time to weigh taxes, traffic and grid strain.
Lakeshore Township blocked data centers using existing zoning on Friday.
Current ordinances already keep large server farms away from homes and wells, so water and noise impacts stay off the table for now.
And that Mid-Michigan town hall on Friday gave residents their first look at power and water demands.
A university-hosted session laid out concrete megawatt and daily water numbers for proposed centers. Nearby communities got to question developers directly.
Now for On Deck, what meetings can listeners actually attend this week?
Tonight, September 8, Ypsilanti City Council holds the second reading and possible adoption of its 60-day emergency moratorium on data center zoning permits.
Tomorrow, September 9, the City of Ionia has an informational meeting on the data center industry and local considerations.
Also tomorrow, University of Michigan hosts a community town hall on the proposed high-performance computing facility in Ypsilanti Township.
And on September 15, Ypsilanti City Council meets again for a public hearing on the zoning ordinance text amendment and that 60-day emergency moratorium.
Plenty of chances for residents to weigh in directly.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Warren's Year-Long Data Center Pause Sparks Regional Pushback Wave
